result: For small alpha the vacant set of a subcritical Boolean model percolates in every d >= 2 (the vacant set percolates whenever the occupied density is below a threshold, a standard continuum percolation fact), so 'unclaimed sites percolate for small alpha' follows from the containment of the claimed set in a Boolean model of radius (1 + o(1)) r_alpha, PROVIDED the territories are indeed within a bounded factor of the free ball: the stable rule can push a territory away from a neighbour but the displaced volume must be absorbed within the region where the free balls overlap, and a chain of displacements has probability decaying geometrically in its length at small alpha, so the containment holds with a radius C r_alpha outside an exceptional set of centres whose density is exponentially small in the chain length. This gives the first question a YES with an argument whose only gap is the chain-of-displacements estimate. For alpha close to 1 the unclaimed set has small density 1 - alpha and is the region left over by the growth process; its percolation is analogous to the vacant set of a nearly-full stable allocation and is expected to fail (density-driven), but there is no monotonicity of the unclaimed set in alpha, which is the obstruction to the second question.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Existence iff det_alpha(A) >= 0 for all finite PSD principal blocks of J_alpha = K(I + alpha K)^{-1} (Maunoury); det_alpha A = (1/n!) sum_lambda dim(lambda) prod_{x in lambda}(1 + c(x) alpha) imm_lambda(A) (Shirai).
method: Reduce the existence question to finite matrices. By Maunoury's Theorem 1 (alpha > 0), an alpha-permanental process with kernel K exists iff Det(I + alpha K_Lambda) >= 1 for all compact Lambda and det_alpha(J_alpha^Lambda(x_i, x_j)) >= 0 a.e. for all n and Lambda, where J_alpha = K(I + alpha K)^{-1}; for K self-adjoint nonnegative and alpha >= 0 the first condition is automatic and J_alpha is again self-adjoint nonnegative with spectrum in [0, 1/alpha), so the conjecture's first half is exactly: det_alpha(A) >= 0 for every real symmetric nonnegative definite matrix A and every alpha in [0, 2].
obstruction: For alpha in (1, 2) not of the form 2/m the only known positive results are for small sizes; the Wishart representation needs an integer number of degrees of freedom, and a continuous-parameter analogue (a 'Wishart law with fractional degrees of freedom' on the cone of PSD matrices) is exactly what is missing: by the Gindikin theorem such laws exist only for degrees of freedom in a discrete set below the dimension, which is the same obstruction in different clothes.
result: Known cases and a small computation. Positivity holds at alpha = 2/m (Shirai's Wishart representation, degrees of freedom m) and at alpha = 1 (permanents of PSD matrices, Marcus-Newman) and alpha = 0 (products of diagonal entries), so the open set of alpha is [0,2] minus {2/m}. For 3 x 3 real symmetric A with unit diagonal and correlations a, b, c: det_alpha A = 1 + alpha(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) + 2 alpha^2 abc, which for a PSD A (1 - a^2 - b^2 - c^2 + 2abc >= 0) is minimised at negative abc; with a = b = 1/2, c = -1/2 (the boundary of the PSD cone, the source's own example up to scaling) it equals 1 + 3 alpha/4 - alpha^2/4, positive exactly for alpha < 4, so no 3 x 3 real counterexample exists below alpha = 4 and Shirai's Theorem 1.2 needs larger matrices for alpha in (2, 4); the real question is therefore whether the minimal size of a counterexample tends to infinity as alpha decreases to 2, which is what the conjecture predicts. A route to the conjecture is the immanant expansion det_alpha A = (1/n!) sum_{|lambda| = n} (dim lambda) c_lambda(alpha) imm_lambda(A) with c_lambda(alpha) = prod_{x in lambda} (1 + c(x) alpha) (Shirai (4.12)), where imm_lambda(A) >= 0 for PSD A (Schur); the coefficients c_lambda(alpha) are nonnegative for all lambda iff alpha <= 1 (the content -1 appears in every lambda with two rows), so for alpha in (1, 2] positivity must come from cancellation between immanants, which is why the hermitian conjecture stops at 1 and the real one at 2 (real symmetric A has imm_lambda(A) = imm_{lambda'}(A) symmetries that pair up the negative coefficients).

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: E exp(i alpha (h(z) - h(w))) is a dimer partition function with monodromy e^{i alpha} around z and w, i.e. a twisted Kasteleyn determinant.
method: Compare with the Gaussian free field limit of h (Kenyon): if h converges to (1/sqrt(pi)) times the GFF in the appropriate normalisation, the formal prediction for the electric field is that of the vertex operators of the free field, E prod_j exp(i alpha_j h(z_j)) proportional to prod_{j<k} |z_j - z_k|^{alpha_j alpha_k g} with g the GFF normalisation constant, after a lattice-dependent multiplicative renormalisation N^{-sum alpha_j^2 g/2}; rotational invariance in the scaling limit is then the statement that the renormalisation constant does not depend on direction.
obstruction: The height function is only defined modulo the lattice conventions and the exponent alpha must be restricted to |alpha| < some threshold for the leading Fisher-Hartwig term to dominate (for larger alpha subleading terms with different monodromies compete and the correlation may oscillate with direction); rotational invariance at the level of the leading exponent is expected in that range only.
result: In lattice directions the Toeplitz/Fisher-Hartwig computation confirms the exponent (the problem says so); off-axis the two-point function of exp(i alpha h) is a 'twisted' dimer partition function (dimers with a phase e^{i alpha} across a cut joining the two points), i.e. a Kasteleyn determinant with a modified weight along a path, whose asymptotics is a determinant of a Toeplitz-like operator with a symbol that has a jump (Fisher-Hartwig singularity) only in lattice directions; in general directions it is a determinant of a 'multiplicatively multivalued' discrete holomorphic problem, which is precisely the framework Dubedat set up (families of Cauchy-Riemann operators, analytic torsion). So the problem reduces to the asymptotics of Kasteleyn determinants with a monodromy e^{i alpha} around two points, and the answer, if Dubedat's analysis covers alpha in the full range, is the free-field vertex operator prediction with rotational invariance.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: k disjoint double-dimer loops crossing A(r,R) force a height-difference change of at least k across the annulus; a sub-Gaussian increment bound with variance C log(R/r) gives the annulus-crossing estimate (r/R)^{c k^2}.
method: The standard route to convergence of a discrete loop ensemble: (a) convergence of finite-dimensional cylindrical observables (done, Basok-Chelkak), (b) tightness in a space of loop configurations (Aizenman-Burchard type), which follows from a bound P(k disjoint loops cross the annulus A(r, R)) <= C (r/R)^{c(k)} with c(k) -> infinity, (c) identification of the limit from (a). Only (b) is missing.
obstruction: The height increment is a linear statistic of the dimer process along a path, and the concentration results for linear statistics of determinantal processes (e.g. Pemantle-Peres, Breuer-Duits) require the statistic to be a sum over points with bounded coefficients of a process with a kernel whose relevant variance is what controls the tail; verifying the hypotheses uniformly in the mesh for the dimer kernel near the boundary of the domain is the technical step, and Temperleyan boundary conditions are needed for (a) but may complicate the boundary behaviour in (b).
result: For double-dimer loops (b) reduces to a height-function estimate. The loops are the level lines of the difference h_1 - h_2 of the two dimer height functions, and k disjoint loops crossing A(r, R) force |h_1 - h_2| to change by at least k (in height units) across the annulus. The height difference converges to sqrt(2) times the GFF (Kenyon), whose increment across A(r,R) is Gaussian with variance of order log(R/r), so the continuum prediction is P(k crossings) <= exp(-c k^2/log(R/r)) = (r/R)^{c k^2}, the CLE(4) k-arm exponent up to constants, which is more than enough for Aizenman-Burchard. So tightness follows from: uniformly in the mesh, the dimer height increment across an annulus of modulus log(R/r) has sub-Gaussian tails with variance C log(R/r), P(|h(x) - h(y)| >= t) <= C exp(-c t^2/log(R/r)) for |x - y| of order R and the two points at distance r from the boundary... in the discrete model the increment is a sum of mean-zero dependent terms with a determinantal structure, and the required estimate is an exponential-moment bound for dimer height increments, which I believe follows from the known variance bounds plus the fact that the height increment is a linear statistic of a determinantal process (hence has Gaussian-type concentration by the results on linear statistics of determinantal processes); if so, (b) holds and the conjecture follows from (a)-(c), including the Hausdorff dimension 3/2 = 1 + kappa/8 for CLE(4) loops.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: The parafermionic observable is half-preholomorphic exactly at x = x_c(n) = 1/sqrt(2 + sqrt(2 - n)), which yields non-exponential decay of arc weights at that point for all n in [0,2] by the Duminil-Copin-Smirnov summation.
method: Use the parafermionic observable F(z) = sum over configurations with an arc from a to z of x^{#edges} n^{#loops} e^{-i sigma W(arc)} with spin sigma = sigma(n) solving the Nienhuis relation; it satisfies half of the discrete Cauchy-Riemann equations (the sum of F around each hexagon vanishes) exactly at x = x_c(n) for every n in [-2, 2], with the constant x_c(n) forced by the local relation. Duminil-Copin and Smirnov turned this into the connective constant for n = 0 by a counting argument that needs the absence of loops.
obstruction: There is no monotonicity of the loop O(n) model in x for n != 1 (no FKG in general; Duminil-Copin-Glazman-Peled-Spinka have it only for n >= 1 and x <= 1/sqrt n), so 'the critical value' is not even a priori a threshold, and exponential decay below x_c(n) has to be proved for each x separately; the known tools (Peierls-type for large n, Ising comparison near n = 1) do not reach the whole interval (0, x_c(n)) for a fixed n in (0,2].
result: What the observable gives for general n at x = x_c(n): summing the vanishing hexagon relation over a domain yields an identity between weighted sums of arcs ending on different parts of the boundary, and since all terms are nonnegative after choosing the domain (a strip or a trapezoid, as in the n = 0 proof) one gets that the arc weights from a boundary point to the far boundary are bounded below by a positive constant uniformly in the domain size, i.e. NO exponential decay at x = x_c(n): the probability that the arc from a reaches distance L does not decay exponentially. This is the direction 'x_c(n) is at most the true critical point' and works for all n in [0, 2] with the same proof as for n = 0 provided the sign structure of the boundary terms is as in the SAW case, which is where loops enter: the loops contribute to the weight but not to the winding, so the terms stay nonnegative. The other direction, exponential decay for x < x_c(n), is where the SAW proof uses that the partition function of walks is dominated by a geometric series in x/x_c and has no analogue with loops.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: H(S) <= log 2 + log 15 sum_{scales k} sum_{dyadic boxes B at scale k} P(S intersects B) for any random set S; for the crossing event the box marginals decay like alpha_4(r,n), making the sum O(n^{3/4}) = O(I(f)).
method: Bound the entropy of a random subset S of the n x n box by a dyadic encoding: write pattern_k for the set of dyadic boxes of side n 2^{-k} that intersect S. By the chain rule H(S) = H(pattern_0) + sum_k H(pattern_{k+1} | pattern_k), and given pattern_k, pattern_{k+1} is determined by choosing, for each occupied box at level k, the nonempty subset of its four children that are occupied (15 possibilities), so H(pattern_{k+1} | pattern_k) <= (log 15) E[N_k] where N_k is the number of occupied boxes at level k. Hence H(S) <= log 2 + log 15 sum_k sum_{B at level k} P(S intersects B). This holds for ANY random set S; the entropy-influence question for a given f is therefore a question about the one-box marginals of the spectral sample at all scales.
obstruction: The whole weight rests on the spectral-sample box estimate P(S intersects B) <= C alpha_4(r,n): the trivial first moment gives only P(S intersects B) <= E|S intersect B| = sum_{i in B} Inf_i(f), which is larger by a factor r^{3/4} and yields only the known general bound H(S) = O(I(f) log n). If Garban-Pete-Schramm's estimate is stated for boxes at distance at least r from the boundary only, the boundary boxes need the separate half-plane bound written above, which I did not verify in their paper.
result: For the percolation crossing event this reduces both inequalities to the box-intersection estimates of Garban, Pete and Schramm (Acta Math. 2010). For a box B of side r in the bulk, P(P(f) intersects B) is at most a constant times the four-arm probability alpha_4(r, n) (a pivotal in B needs four alternating arms from B to distance of order n), and, as I recall their first-moment section, they prove the same upper bound for the spectral sample, P(S(f) intersects B) <= C alpha_4(r, n); boxes touching the boundary have the half-plane three-arm bound (r/n)^2 and contribute at most O(1) per scale. With alpha_4(r,n) of order (r/n)^{5/4} on the triangular lattice, the level-k sum is (n/r)^2 (r/n)^{5/4} = (n/r)^{3/4} = 2^{3k/4}, a geometric series dominated by the finest scale, so sum_k sum_B P(S intersects B) <= C n^{3/4} <= C' I(f) since I(f) = n^2 alpha_4(1, n) is of order n^{3/4}. The same computation with the pivotal set gives H(P(f)) <= C I(f). If the recalled box estimate for the spectral sample is as stated (upper bound by a constant times the four-arm probability, uniformly over bulk boxes of all sizes r <= n), this settles both inequalities of Conjecture 8 on the triangular lattice, with constants; on Z^2 the same argument gives H = O(I(f)) as soon as the spectral-sample box estimate holds with any polynomial decay alpha_4(r,n) <= (r/n)^{1+delta}, which is what quasi-multiplicativity and the a priori bound alpha_4(r,n) <= C (r/n)^{1+delta} (from the five-arm exponent 2 and Reimer) give. I have not re-read Garban-Pete-Schramm to confirm the exact form of their one-box first-moment estimate; that check is the only thing between this argument and a proof, so the row is flagged as a partial result rather than a solution.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: P(f(x) != f(x^epsilon)) <= epsilon I(f) for any f (hybrid argument), which settles the AND/OR analogue via Boppana but not the threshold case, where majority has I of order sqrt(M) yet is stable.
method: Compare with what total influence gives. For any Boolean f and product noise, the hybrid argument gives P(f(x) != f(x^epsilon)) <= epsilon I(f). Boppana's theorem bounds I(f) <= C (log M)^{D-1} for monotone AND/OR circuits, so the AND/OR analogue of part (i) is immediate with t = (log M)^D. For threshold gates the influence route fails at depth one already: majority of M inputs has I = c sqrt(M) but is stable to 1/t-noise for every t -> infinity (Peres: linear threshold functions have noise sensitivity at most C sqrt(epsilon)). So part (i) is a statement about the Fourier tail beyond the influence, and it needs a composition principle for noise stability under monotone threshold gates.
obstruction: There is no composition theorem for noise stability of threshold gates with dependent input noise, and the known techniques (hypercontractivity for the Fourier tail, Peres' argument for a single gate, Boppana/Hastad influence bounds for AND/OR) each break at the second level of threshold gates; part (ii) additionally allows negative weights inside a monotone function, for which no structural result exists at all, consistent with the source calling it reckless.
result: Reduction of part (i) to a 'robust Peres theorem'. Feed a depth-D circuit bottom-up: at the first level each gate g_j is a linear threshold function of the inputs, and Peres gives P(g_j(x) != g_j(x^epsilon)) <= C sqrt(epsilon). At the second level a gate g receives inputs y = (g_j(x)) and y' = (g_j(x^epsilon)) which differ in each coordinate with probability at most C sqrt(epsilon), but the coordinates' disagreements are neither independent nor independent of y. If a linear threshold function satisfied P(g(y) != g(y')) <= C sqrt(max_j P(y_j != y'_j)) for every coupling of this kind, induction would give P(f(x) != f(x^epsilon)) <= C^D epsilon^{2^{-D}}, i.e. stability to 1/t-noise for t = t(D) -> infinity, which is qualitatively part (i) with a far worse dependence than (log M)^{100D}: the conjectured polylogarithmic t is then a quantitative statement that bounded-depth composition amplifies noise only polylogarithmically in the size. For general couplings the robust Peres statement is false (an adversary flips the largest-weight input), so the induction must use that the disagreements produced by the lower levels are 'random-like' with respect to g's weights, which is where the monotonicity and the polylogarithmic bound on influences of the lower gates should enter.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Parity shows C >= 1 is necessary; Friedgut's junta theorem gives the conjecture with a doubly exponential size at depth 2.
method: Calibrate the statement against known functions. Parity on k variables has I = k and, by Hastad's lower bound, needs size exp(c k^{1/(d-1)}) in depth d, so any C >= 1 is consistent and C < 1 is excluded: the conjecture says parity is the hardest function for its influence. Majority on n bits has I of order sqrt(n) and is 0.01-approximable by depth-2 circuits (DNF) of size exp(O(sqrt(n))), i.e. log M of order I(f), consistent. Friedgut's junta theorem gives, for every f with I(f) = k, a 0.01-approximating junta on exp(O(k)) variables, hence a depth-2 circuit of size exp(exp(O(k))): this proves the conjecture with log M replaced by log log M, a doubly exponential loss, and shows the conjecture is a strengthening of Friedgut's theorem at depth 2: every function of influence k is close to a DNF of size exp(k^{O(1)}), not just to a junta on exp(O(k)) variables.
obstruction: The junta theorem is the only general structural consequence of small total influence, and it loses an exponential; bridging exp(exp(O(k))) and exp(k^{O(1)}) needs an approximation theory for bounded-depth circuits driven by Fourier concentration at low levels (small influence implies most spectral weight at levels <= O(k)), and low-degree Fourier concentration is known to give bounded-depth approximators only for functions that are already in AC0 (Linial-Mansour-Nisan is the converse direction).
result: At depth d = 2 the conjecture is equivalent to: every Boolean f with I(f) = k is 0.01-close to a DNF of size exp(k^{C'}). Known: Friedgut's junta is a function of exp(O(k)) variables and can be written as a DNF of size exp(exp(O(k))); a monotone f with I(f) = k is close to a function of exp(O(k)) variables with the same influence bound, and the question is whether the junta's own structure can be exploited. Test case: the 'tribes' function (a DNF with terms of size log n - log log n) has I of order log n and is itself a DNF of size n = exp(O(I)), consistent. A candidate counterexample must have small influence and no small DNF approximation: address/multiplexer-type functions have influence O(log n) and DNF size polynomial in n = exp(O(I)), again consistent. I found no candidate violating exp(k^{C'}) at depth 2, and the depth-d version reduces to depth 2 only if one accepts a loss in the exponent, so the conjecture is plausible and unresolved.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: I(X_n ; Y_n) <= H(X_n) - H(X_n | (g_i)_{i not in R}); l^1-noise sensitivity forces the shared increments to carry o(1) information about the endpoint.
method: Write X_n = g_1 ... g_n and Y_n = g'_1 ... g'_n where g'_i = g_i off the resampled set R (a Bernoulli(epsilon) subset of {1, ..., n}) and independent otherwise. The two necessary conditions are visible from this: a homomorphism phi: Gamma -> Z gives phi(X_n) - phi(Y_n) = sum_{i in R} (phi(g_i) - phi(g'_i)), a sum of about epsilon n independent terms, while phi(X_n) itself has variance of order n, so (phi(X_n), phi(Y_n)) has correlation 1 - epsilon in the limit; and if the Poisson boundary is nontrivial the first steps bias both endpoints toward the same boundary point. The conjecture says nothing else can correlate the endpoints.
obstruction: All known tools for Liouville groups (entropy criterion, Poisson boundary triviality) are asymptotic and insensitive to an epsilon-fraction of the increments; a proof of noise sensitivity needs a quantitative mixing statement for the 'shared-increment' sigma-field at finite n, and no such technique exists even for the simplest intermediate-growth examples. The obstruction from Z-quotients shows that any proof must use the absence of virtual homomorphisms to Z, a purely algebraic condition whose probabilistic meaning (beyond the CLT along the homomorphism) is not understood.
result: A reduction to a finite-n entropy statement. Let H_n = H(X_n) be the entropy of the walk and consider H(X_n | (g_i)_{i not in R}), the residual entropy of the endpoint given the shared increments. Total variation independence of (X_n, Y_n) implies I(X_n ; Y_n) -> 0, and since Y_n is a function of the shared increments and independent extra ones, I(X_n ; Y_n) <= I(X_n ; (g_i)_{i not in R}) = H_n - H(X_n | shared increments). So l^1-noise sensitivity requires H(X_n | shared increments) = H_n - o(1): resampling an epsilon-fraction of the steps must destroy essentially all information about the endpoint, which for Liouville groups (H_n = o(n)) is a statement about how the sublinear entropy is distributed along the word. In the abelian case the shared increments determine X_n up to the sum of epsilon n independent steps, whose entropy is of order log(epsilon n), while H_n is of order log n: the residual entropy is H_n - O(1)... which is why abelian groups fail only at the level of the normalised position, not of entropy; this is exactly why Benjamini-Brieussel separate the l^1 and entropy notions. For the Grigorchuk group the walk entropy grows like n^{alpha} with alpha < 1 (Erschler-type bounds), and the conjecture predicts that conjugation by the shared prefixes scrambles the resampled increments enough that no O(1) statistic of X_n survives.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: BKS: Var(D) <= C sum_e Inf_e(D)^2 / (typical spectral level); noise sensitivity at level n^{-delta} would give Var(D) = O(n^{1-c}).
method: Separate the two notions the question conflates: (a) noise sensitivity at fixed epsilon (Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm criterion sum_e Inf_e(f)^2 -> 0), and (b) sensitivity at polynomial noise epsilon = n^{-delta}, which is what would improve the variance bound. Both are statements about the Fourier spectrum of f = 1{D >= M}: (a) says the spectral sample S_f has |S_f| -> infinity in probability, (b) says |S_f| >= n^{delta} with probability 1 - o(1), and by the BKS argument Var(D) <= C n / (typical spectral level), roughly.
obstruction: Every quantitative tool (hypercontractivity/BKS, randomised algorithms as in Schramm-Steif) needs either a bound on the largest influence at polynomial scale or a randomised algorithm that computes f while querying each edge with polynomially small probability; for the crossing event such an algorithm exists (exploration path), for D there is no known algorithm that determines D >= M without examining a positive fraction of the corridor with probability bounded below, which is exactly the localisation of geodesics that is not controlled beyond n^{1/2+o(1)}... (transversal fluctuation upper bounds are only known at that level), so the method that worked for percolation has no known analogue here.
result: The influence of an edge e on f is at most P(e lies on a geodesic) times P(a unit change of D crosses the median | e on the geodesic) <= C (1/n)-ish times n^{-chi} where n^{chi} is the scale of the fluctuations of D, using that geodesics have n^{1+o(1)} edges spread over the corridor; so sum_e Inf_e^2 <= n^{1+2xi} (n^{-1-chi})^2 -> 0 where n^{xi} is the transversal fluctuation scale (2 xi = chi + 1 under the KPZ relation predicts 1 + 4/3 - 2 - 2/3 < 0), which gives (a) once the a priori bounds P(e on geodesic) <= n^{-1+o(1)} on average and Var(D) >= n^{2chi} with chi > 0 are available; the second is not known (Var(D) >= c log n is the only lower bound), so even (a) is conditional. For (b), a KPZ heuristic predicts the spectral level: D is a sum of order n^{1/3} approximately independent contributions from corridor segments of length n^{2/3}, each with O(n^{1/3}) fluctuations, so f = 1{D >= M} should behave like a majority-type function of n^{1/3} nearly independent blocks, each block being itself a function of n^{2/3 + 2 xi} edges; majority of m independent bits has spectral level of order... its spectral sample is of size O(1) with probability bounded below, so the above-median function is expected to be noise STABLE at the block level and sensitive only through the internal structure of the blocks: the prediction is sensitivity at noise level epsilon = n^{-delta} for some delta > 0 iff within a block of length n^{2/3} the passage time is polynomially noise sensitive, a self-similar reduction with no base case.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Achlioptas-Friedgut sharpness reduces the conjecture to the existence of lim_n d_k(n); for k >= k_0 the limit is the condensation-threshold formula.
method: Split the conjecture into sharpness and convergence. Achlioptas-Friedgut give a sharp threshold: for each k there are d_k(n) with P(chi <= k) jumping from o(1) to 1 - o(1) in a window of width o(1) around d_k(n). So the conjecture is exactly the statement that lim_n d_k(n) exists for every k, the same 'convergence of the threshold sequence' question as for random k-SAT.
obstruction: Convergence of d_k(n) requires identifying the limit, and for small k the limit is predicted by a replica-symmetry-breaking formula whose rigorous derivation needs the full condensation picture (Bapst, Coja-Oghlan, Hetterich, Rassmann, Vilenchik for large k) at small k, where the 1-RSB prediction is believed exact but the proof techniques (contiguity and planted-model arguments) rely on large-k expansions.
result: For k large the limit exists and is known: Coja-Oghlan-Vilenchik pin the threshold to within o_k(1), and for random regular graphs Coja-Oghlan-Efthymiou-Hetterich identify it exactly (as the condensation/one-step-replica-symmetry-breaking prediction) for k >= k_0; on G(n, d/n) the exact identification for large k follows the same route (the 'cavity' formula) and I believe is done in the same line of work, which would make the conjecture true for k >= k_0 and open for small k, with k = 3 (predicted d_3 = 4.687...) the first open case. For small k the available bounds sandwich the threshold in an interval of positive length (e.g. for k = 3, between 4.03 and 4.937 by second-moment and first-moment arguments), and the second moment method, which gave Achlioptas-Naor's two values, provably cannot reach the exact threshold because of the condensation transition below it.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: At c = 3/2 the model is the random cubic graph (Robinson-Wormald); above it the model is contiguous with a configuration model with a truncated-Poisson degree sequence of unbounded maximum degree.
method: Identify why c = 3/2 is the natural boundary: 2m >= 3n forces c >= 3/2, and at c = 3/2 exactly the graph is a random cubic graph, Hamiltonian w.h.p. by Robinson-Wormald's small-subgraph-conditioning second moment computation. For c slightly above 3/2 the degree sequence of G_{n,cn;3} is a truncated Poisson (conditioned to be >= 3) with mean 2c, so the graph is a random graph with a given degree sequence whose maximum degree is of order log n / log log n.
obstruction: The Posa-rotation approach of Frieze and Anastos-Frieze is capped at c = 2.662 by the expansion properties of 2-matchings, and the second-moment approach has never been carried out with unbounded degrees; a proof for c in (3/2, 2.662] needs one of the two to be pushed beyond its known limit, and the second is the natural one given that the c = 3/2 case is exactly Robinson-Wormald.
result: Reduction: the conjecture follows from Hamiltonicity w.h.p. of the configuration-model random graph with the truncated-Poisson degree sequence of mean 2c, for every c > 3/2, by contiguity of G_{n,cn;3} with that model; for degree sequences with minimum degree 3 and BOUNDED maximum degree, Hamiltonicity w.h.p. is known (Cooper-Frieze-Reed 2002 for regular and near-regular, via the Robinson-Wormald method), and the only obstacle for the truncated-Poisson sequence is the unbounded maximum degree. So the conjecture is equivalent to extending the Robinson-Wormald second-moment/small-subgraph-conditioning computation for the number of Hamilton cycles to degree sequences with maximum degree of order log n / log log n, which is where the variance of the number of Hamilton cycles picks up contributions from the high-degree vertices that the current computations cannot control.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Friedgut sharpness + Ding-Sly-Sun for large k; the open content is lim_n c_k(n) for 3 <= k < k_0.
method: As for the chromatic number: Friedgut's sharp threshold theorem reduces the conjecture to the convergence of the threshold sequence c_k(n) defined by P(satisfiable) = 1/2, and convergence has only ever been proved by identifying the limit.
obstruction: The Ding-Sly-Sun argument uses k large in essentially every estimate (moment computations of clusters, contiguity of the planted model); nobody has a technique that proves convergence of a threshold sequence without computing it, and the computation for k = 3 requires the 1-RSB machinery to be controlled at small k where the physics prediction, though believed, has no rigorous foundation.
result: For k >= k_0 the limit is the 1-RSB prediction (Ding-Sly-Sun), proved through the survey-propagation/condensation structure of the solution space, which is rigorous only when k is large enough for the 'frozen variables' picture to be established by first and second moment computations with large-k expansions. For small k the same formula is believed exact, and the proof would need the same structural statements (the solution space is a union of well-separated clusters with frozen variables above the condensation threshold) without the large-k expansions; for k = 3 the second moment method fails already at c of order 2^k ln 2 - O(k), far below the predicted threshold, because of the condensation transition. A different route to mere existence of the limit (without its value) would be a monotonicity or self-averaging argument in n, which does not exist: Friedgut's sharpness gives the window but not the location, and the location can in principle oscillate.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: beta_2 = E[per-point length of the local limit of optimal tours] if the local limit exists (objective method); the lower bound uses that both tour edges at a point are at least the nearest-neighbour distance.
method: Ask what 'determine' can mean. beta_2 = lim E L_n/sqrt(n) is, by the Aldous-Steele objective method, the expected per-point length of an optimal 'infinite tour' of the unit-intensity Poisson process if such a translation-invariant local limit of optimal tours exists; the constant would then be an expectation over a translation-invariant random structure on the Poisson process, for which a closed form is not expected. So the realistic content of the problem is (a) existence and description of the local limit of optimal tours, and (b) sharper rigorous bounds.
obstruction: The optimal tour has no local characterisation (unlike the MST, which is determined locally by the cycle criterion), so every known tool gives only bounds; exact determination would need an unexpected exact solvability, and there is no evidence for it.
result: (a) is itself open: it is not known that the optimal tours on n points converge locally (in the Aldous-Steele sense) to a translation-invariant infinite path on the Poisson process, nor that such a limit is unique; the analogous statement for the minimal spanning tree is known (it converges to the Poisson MSF, single tree or not being a separate open question already in the campaign as C0113). If (a) held, beta_2 = E[half the sum of the two edge lengths at the origin of the limit tour] by mass transport, and the bounds in (b) would become questions about the local structure of the limit. (b): the lower bound 0.625 comes from comparing with the minimal matching/nearest-neighbour graph (each point has two tour edges each at least the nearest-neighbour distance, with a refinement for the second edge), and the upper bound from explicit constructions (space-filling curve heuristics improved by local optimisation); improving either needs a structural property of optimal tours, e.g. the distribution of the angle between the two tour edges at a point, which is unknown.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Objective-method RDE: X = min over Poisson edges of (w - Y^{(1)} - Y^{(2)}), the three-dimensional analogue of the logistic RDE of the random assignment problem.
method: Compare the two bounds with the two-dimensional case to see which is the truth. Lower bound: each of the n matching edges costs at least the minimum of the n^2 weights at one of its vertices, giving Z_n >= c/n. Upper bound: keep only edges of weight at most p = C log n / n^2, i.e. a random 3-uniform hypergraph with about n^3 p = C n log n edges, which by Johansson-Kahn-Vu has a perfect matching w.h.p., so Z_n <= n p = C log n / n. In two dimensions the analogous bounds are c/n <= Z_n <= C log n/n... times n, and the truth, Aldous's zeta(2), sits at the LOWER bound's order: the optimal matching uses edges cheaper on average than the threshold edges. So the natural conjecture is Z_n = Theta(1/n), and more precisely that n Z_n converges to a constant c_3 given by a recursive distributional equation on the local weak limit of the weighted hypergraph.
obstruction: Aldous's zeta(2) proof needs (i) endogeny/uniqueness for the RDE and (ii) a local-convergence argument that the finite optimal matching is close to the limit matching, using the bipartite graph structure (alternating paths); for hypergraph matchings there is no alternating-path augmentation structure, so (ii) has no known proof strategy, and even the existence of the limit c_3 is open.
result: The objective-method reduction: rescaling weights by n^2, the neighbourhood of a vertex in H_{n:3} with weights n^2 X_e converges to a Poisson-weighted infinite hypertree (each vertex has a Poisson process of rate 1 of incident edges, each edge having two other vertices with their own independent hypertrees). If the minimum-weight perfect matching converges locally to an invariant perfect matching of this limit object (the analogue of Aldous's zeta(2) argument), then lim n Z_n = c_3 = E[weight of the edge covering the root]/3 and c_3 is characterised by the recursive distributional equation for the 'cost of not matching the root': X = min_e (w_e - Y_e^{(1)} - Y_e^{(2)}) over the Poisson edges at the root with Y independent copies of X (two subtrees per edge instead of one), the three-dimensional analogue of the logistic RDE whose solution gives zeta(2). Writing the RDE and checking whether it has a unique solution with the right tail (the two-dimensional solution is logistic) is the concrete next step; the answer would give Z_n = (c_3 + o(1))/n, refuting the log n upper bound as the truth.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Existence of the matching is dual to a uniform empirical-process bound over a function class with mixed Orlicz derivative constraints; 1/alpha_1 + 1/alpha_2 = 1/2 is the critical-entropy condition.
method: Write the conjecture as a transport-duality statement. A matching with the two Orlicz-type constraints exists iff the empirical measures of the X's and Y's are close in the transport distance whose cost is the Orlicz norm defined by the two exponents; by duality that is a uniform bound on sup_f |sum_i f(X_i) - f(Y_i)| over the class of functions f on the square whose partial derivatives satisfy the dual Orlicz constraints, which is the class the source describes ('a certain class of functions defined through a control of the partial derivatives'); the conjecture is then a bound on the expected supremum of an empirical process, i.e. on gamma_2 of that class in L^2([0,1]^2).
obstruction: The chaining/generic-chaining bound gamma_2 for the dual class is not known to be of order sqrt(log N) when the two derivative constraints have different Orlicz exponents; the known proofs of AKT (Fourier/transport) and of Leighton-Shor (dyadic grids) each exploit a structure specific to one exponent, and the source states that even the conjunction of the two known theorems for a single matching is unproved.
result: Calibration. The AKT theorem (alpha_1 = alpha_2 = 1... in the L^1 form) and the Leighton-Shor theorem (the sup form) each control one member of the family of dual classes, and the conjecture asks for the whole family at once with the exponents coupled by 1/alpha_1 + 1/alpha_2 = 1/2, which is the condition under which the corresponding function class has 'critical' entropy (its gamma_2 functional is of order sqrt(log N), the same as for the AKT class). The coupling is sharp: if 1/alpha_1 + 1/alpha_2 > 1/2 the class is larger and the bound is known to fail by the lower bounds for AKT-type matchings. A concrete partial: the case alpha_1 = infinity, alpha_2 = 2 requires a matching with max_i |X_i^1 - Y_{pi(i)}^1| <= L sqrt(log N/N) in the first coordinate and a Gaussian-type Orlicz control in the second; the first coordinate condition alone is easy (sort both samples by the first coordinate and match in order: the i-th order statistics differ by O(sqrt(log N/N)) w.h.p. by the DKW inequality), and the whole difficulty is that this order-matching has second-coordinate discrepancies of order 1, so any proof must interleave the two coordinates at every dyadic scale, exactly as the Leighton-Shor grid argument does, but with an L^2-type rather than sup-type accounting in the second coordinate.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: For a codimension-k subcube, sup_t t lambda(f * mu >= t) is attained at a = k(1/2 + epsilon) where the exponential rate cancels exactly, leaving a prefactor of order 1/sqrt(k) = c/sqrt(log t).
method: Compute the extremal examples exactly to see what rate is conjectured. Take f = 2^k 1_A with A = {x : x_1 = ... = x_k = 1} a subcube of codimension k, and mu the biased coin with mu(1) = 1/2 + epsilon. Then (f * mu)(x) = 2^k (1/2 + epsilon)^a (1/2 - epsilon)^{k-a} where a is the number of i <= k with x_i = 1, and lambda(f * mu >= t) is a binomial tail P(Bin(k, 1/2) >= a(t)).
obstruction: The remaining log log factor in Chen and Xiang-Zhang comes from a stochastic-localisation/perturbed-reverse-heat argument whose error terms are not dimension-free at the polynomial scale; closing it needs a genuinely new estimate for the level sets of T_mu f at the scale where the subcube computation is tight, and the source itself expects the problem to be hard ('I do not think that the problem by itself has any importance. It is just pretty.').
result: With a = k(1/2 + u), log(t lambda(f * mu >= t)) = k[ (1/2) log(1 - 4 epsilon^2) + u log((1+2 epsilon)/(1-2 epsilon)) - I(u) ] + O(log k), where I(u) = (1/2+u) log(1+2u) + (1/2-u) log(1-2u) is the binomial rate function; the bracket is maximised at u = epsilon and there it equals EXACTLY zero (direct algebra: the three terms cancel identically). So for subcubes the supremum over levels of t lambda(f * mu >= t) is governed by the polynomial prefactor of the local limit theorem: it is of order 1/sqrt(k) at the level t = exp(c(epsilon) k), i.e. t phi(t) >= c/sqrt(log t) is forced. This shows (a) the conjecture, if true, is sharp only at the rate 1/sqrt(log t), the rate now proved up to log log factors; (b) subcubes are near-extremal, matching the one-dimensional Gaussian computation of Ball-Barthe-Bednorz-Oleszkiewicz-Wolff; (c) any proof must beat the exponential-scale cancellation and control the polynomial prefactor uniformly in N, which is why hypercontractivity (which only sees exponential scales, and does not map L^1 anywhere useful) is not enough.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: A(q) is an up-class; sum over minimal M in A(q) of p^{card M} <= 1/2 is sufficient for p-smallness and is the expected number of minimal non-coverable subsets of a p-random set.
method: Use that A(q) is an up-class (a set that cannot be covered by q members of A has no coverable superset), so p-smallness has a sufficient condition in terms of its minimal elements: if sum over the minimal elements M of A(q) of p^{card M} <= 1/2 then A(q) is p-small (cover by the H_M). Equivalently: the expected number of minimal non-coverable subsets of a mu_p-random set is at most 1/2. So the conjecture would follow from: mu_p(A) >= 1 - 1/q implies E_p[number of minimal elements of A(q) contained in X] <= 1/2.
obstruction: p-smallness is a covering property, and the minimal-element cover is only one candidate; the source's own comment is that there is no 'magic wand' producing the covering family, and the withdrawn 2025 proof attempt indicates that the natural first-moment arguments do not close. The weakly-small version (Conjecture 7.2) is the natural intermediate target and is itself open.
result: Two checks of this sufficient condition. (1) A = {emptyset}: A(q) = {Y != emptyset}, minimal elements are the singletons, the expected count is Np, not small, yet the conjecture only applies if mu_p(A) = (1-p)^N >= 1 - 1/q, i.e. Np <= 1/q roughly, in which case Np <= 1/2: consistent. (2) A = {X : card X <= m} with mu_p(A) >= 1 - 1/q, i.e. m >= Np + C sqrt(Np): A(q) = {Y : card Y > qm} (a set of size > qm cannot be covered by q sets of size <= m, and one of size <= qm can), minimal elements are the sets of size qm + 1, expected count binom(N, qm+1) p^{qm+1} <= (eNp/(qm+1))^{qm+1} <= (e/q)^{qm+1}, at most 1/2 for q >= 6: consistent, and this example shows the constant q cannot be 2 for small p (with q = 2 the count is (e/2)^{2m+1}, large). So the minimal-element sufficient condition survives the natural examples and suggests the true statement is a 'second moment' one: large classes have few minimal non-coverable sets. Its failure would need a class A of measure near 1 whose non-coverable sets have many small minimal elements, i.e. many small sets each of which meets the complement of every q-fold union of members of A, which forces the q-fold unions to miss a positive density of points, contradicting mu_p(A) large only heuristically (the union of q independent samples from A conditioned on A covers each point with probability 1 - (1-p)^q... this is the calculation that Lemma 7.4 of the source makes precise for measures, not for covers).

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Conjecture 7.2 iff no (2p)-spread measure on A(q); unconditioned q-fold unions cover J with probability (1-(1-p)^q)^{card J}.
method: Use the source's duality (Proposition 6.5): Conjecture 7.2 is equivalent to: if mu_p(A) >= 1 - 1/q then A(q) carries no (2p)-spread probability measure. So the conjecture is a statement about spread measures supported on non-coverable sets, and the source's Propositions 7.6-7.7 show it follows from the thinning conjecture 7.3.
obstruction: The union of q independent p-random sets is a (1-(1-p)^q)-random set, so with constant q it covers a set J of size card J >> 1/p with exponentially small probability, and the conditioning on A must be what makes covering likely; no tool expresses 'conditioned on a large up-class' as a spread condition, which is the whole content of Conjecture 7.3.
result: A direct attack via the spread measure. Suppose nu is (2p)-spread and supported on A(q); for J drawn from nu and X_1, ..., X_q i.i.d. from mu_p conditioned on A, the event {J subset of X_1 u ... u X_q} has probability zero. But for a (2p)-spread nu, the source's Corollary 11.4 / (6.7) says that a p-random set X satisfies E sup_{J} card(X intersect J) >= (typical size)/L... more to the point, for J fixed, P(J subset of X_1 u ... u X_q) = (1 - (1-p)^q)^{card J} for UNCONDITIONED X_i, which is tiny when card J is large, so the conditioning on A (an event of probability >= 1 - 1/q) cannot lower it by more than a factor q^q... and a contradiction would need P(J subset of union) to be at least q^{-q}-ish for some J in the support of nu, i.e. card J <= C log q/p: the conjecture therefore reduces to showing that a (2p)-spread measure on A(q) can be assumed supported on sets of size O_q(1/p), a 'size reduction' for spread measures on up-classes. For sets J of size at most C/p, (1 - (1-p)^q)^{card J} >= exp(-C (1-p)^q/p) is bounded below when q >= C' log(1/p)/p, which is not a constant q. So the naive first-moment route gives the conjecture only with q growing like log(1/p)/p, and the constant-q statement is exactly what the source's 'daring' Conjectures 7.3 and 7.9 are designed to capture.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Fractional cover: sum_{I subset of T} g(I) >= 1 for T in A with sum_I g(I) p^{card I} <= 1/2; the question is a constant integrality gap after the geometric relaxation p -> p/L.
method: Read the problem as an integrality gap. Weakly p-small means a fractional cover g of A by cylinders H_I with total weight sum_I g(I) p^{card I} <= 1/2 and sum_{I subset of T} g(I) >= 1 for each T in A; (p/L)-small means an integral cover with weight sum_I (p/L)^{card I} <= 1/2. The question is whether this covering LP has a bounded integrality gap once the weights are relaxed geometrically (p -> p/L), i.e. whether a fractional cover of cost 1/2 at parameter p can be rounded to an integral cover of cost 1/2 at parameter p/L. Randomised rounding (include I with probability proportional to g(I)) covers each T only with probability bounded away from 1, and boosting by a log factor is the Kahn-Kalai log; the conjecture says a smarter rounding loses only a constant in the exponent base.
obstruction: The reduction to bounded size is heuristic: the fractional mass on T can be spread over sizes in a way that no single size class carries a constant fraction, and the large-I cylinders that become cheap under p/L may not cover the same T's efficiently once rounded; FKP's pairs argument uses graph-theoretic structure (matchings and degrees) with no evident hypergraph analogue, which is why the size-3 case is already unresolved.
result: What the geometric relaxation buys: replacing p by p/L multiplies the cost of a cylinder H_I by L^{-card I}, so cylinders with large I become almost free, and the natural rounding is: for each T in A, the fractional cover gives sum_{I subset of T} g(I) >= 1 with cost weights p^{card I}; sort the I's contained in T by size; if a constant fraction of the fractional mass on T sits on I's of size >= s, then any integral choice of such I's costs at most L^{-s} times their fractional cost at parameter p... this handles the large-I part of the cover and reduces the problem to fractional covers supported on sets of bounded size s_0 = O(log L), which is where Frankston-Kahn-Park's pairs case sits (size 2). So Problem 6.3 reduces to the bounded-size case: for fractional covers by cylinders of size at most s_0, is the integrality gap bounded by a constant depending on s_0? For size 1 it is trivial (a fractional cover by singletons of cost 1/2 has an integral version: take all singletons with g > 0... with cost at most... no: a fractional cover by singletons is an integral cover after removing the singletons with tiny weight, which loses a constant), for size 2 it is FKP's theorem, and the general bounded-size case is a hypergraph covering question with the same flavour.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: For A = {X != emptyset} the class in question is {card J > N log(1-p)/log(1-alpha)}, weakly alpha p-small for alpha small since uniform measures on k-sets are only (k/N)-spread.
method: Test the conjecture on the basic up-classes. For A = {X != emptyset}: theta_{J,alpha}(A) = 1 - (1-alpha)^{card J} exceeds mu_p(A) = 1 - (1-p)^N iff card J > N log(1-p)/log(1-alpha), roughly card J > Np/alpha for small p, alpha. The class {J : card J >= cNp/alpha} is weakly alpha p-small iff it carries no (2 alpha p)-spread measure (Proposition 6.5); the most spread measure on sets of size k is the uniform one, which is (k/N)-spread (source, Section 6), so the class is not weakly small only if k/N <= 2 alpha p with k = cNp/alpha, i.e. only if c <= 2 alpha^2, which fails for small alpha since c is of order 1. So the conjecture holds for this class for alpha small enough, with the mechanism visible: thinning by alpha divides the effective size by alpha while the spread condition only gains a factor alpha.
obstruction: All examples decided here are 'read-once' block structures where the thinning acts coordinatewise; the source's Section 10 shows that block constructions cannot disprove the stronger Conjecture 9.1, and the genuinely open case is an up-class A not built from blocks, e.g. a symmetric class defined by a permutation group orbit, where theta_{J,alpha}(A) has no product formula and neither the conjecture nor a counterexample is accessible by computation.
result: The same computation for A = {X : card X >= m} (threshold classes) gives: theta_{J,alpha}(A) > mu_p(A) iff a Bin(card J, alpha) exceeds m more often than Bin(N, p) does, i.e. iff alpha card J > Np + (fluctuation corrections), so the class is again {card J >= (Np/alpha)(1 + o(1))} and is weakly alpha p-small by the same spread count. For 'union-of-blocks' classes A = {X : X meets every S_i} (S_i disjoint of size r, N = mr), theta_{J,alpha}(A) = prod_i (1 - (1-alpha)^{card(J intersect S_i)}) > mu_p(A) = (1 - (1-p)^r)^m requires J to have roughly (p/alpha) r points in most blocks, and a measure on such J's is (p/alpha)/(1)... the uniform measure on sets meeting each block in exactly (pr/alpha) points is (p/alpha)-spread by the tensorisation remark in the source, which is more spread than 2 alpha p precisely when alpha^2 <= 1/2: consistent again. So every product-type example is consistent with the conjecture, in line with the source's Theorem 11.10 for the multiplicative version.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: W_alpha(nu)(H_I) = alpha^{card I} nu(H_I) <= (alpha^2 p)^{card I}: cylinder domination holds with a factor alpha^{card I} to spare; the conjecture is the upgrade to all up-classes.
method: Compare cylinder marginals first. If nu is alpha p-spread then its alpha-thinning W_alpha(nu) satisfies W_alpha(nu)(H_I) = integral alpha^{card I} 1{I subset of J} dnu(J) = alpha^{card I} nu(H_I) <= (alpha^2 p)^{card I} <= p^{card I} = mu_p(H_I): the thinned measure is dominated by mu_p on every cylinder, with room to spare (a factor alpha^{card I}). The conjecture asks to upgrade domination on cylinders to domination on all up-classes.
obstruction: Domination is a statement about all up-classes simultaneously and has no tensorisation for non-product nu; the source's proposed induction on coordinates lacks an induction hypothesis, and the dual formulation 7.12 asks to construct a measure eta by a 'magic method'. A counterexample would have to come from a spread measure not built from simpler pieces (Theorem 11.10 excludes those), e.g. a group orbit, and testing domination against all up-classes for such a nu is computationally out of reach beyond tiny S.
result: Domination on cylinders does not imply domination on up-classes in general (the source's singleton example: uniform nu on singletons has nu(H_I) <= 1/M for all nonempty I yet gives mass 1 to the up-class {X != emptyset} whose mu_p-measure is 1 - (1-p)^M < 1), and the thinning is exactly what repairs the example: W_alpha(nu)({X != emptyset}) = alpha while mu_p({X != emptyset}) >= alpha once p >= alpha/M... and the spread condition alpha p >= 1/M gives p >= 1/(alpha M), so mu_p({X != emptyset}) >= 1 - e^{-1/alpha} >= alpha for alpha <= 1/2: the example is consistent for a reason, not by accident. The general mechanism: for an up-class A with minimal elements of typical size s, mu_p(A) >= 1 - e^{-(number of minimal elements) p^s}-type bounds (Janson) versus W_alpha(nu)(A) <= sum over minimal M of alpha^{card M} nu(H_M) <= (alpha^2 p)^s (number of minimal elements); so domination holds when the minimal elements are few enough that mu_p(A) is already of order (number) p^s, and when they are many the Janson lower bound for mu_p(A) saturates near 1; the dangerous intermediate regime is where the minimal elements overlap heavily (Janson's Delta term large), and that is where neither bound is sharp. This is the same regime that makes Kahn-Kalai hard, and the conjecture is a domination-strengthening of the Kahn-Kalai family: the source shows 8.5 (with delta = p this is 7.9) implies 8.2, which is now a theorem (FKNP), so 7.9 is consistent with everything proved.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Both endpoints are theorems: s = 1 is the source's (6.7), s of order log m is FKNP Theorem 1.6; the conjecture is the exponential interpolation, plausibly obtained by stopping the FKNP iteration after s rounds.
method: Locate 8.4 between two theorems. At p = delta (s := p/delta = 1) the conjecture asks E_p(B) >= m(1 - L/e), i.e. some member of B has a constant fraction of its points in a p-random set, which is the source's own (6.7) (Corollary 11.4): E_p(B) >= m/L for p-spread measures. At p >= L delta log(m+1), i.e. s of order log m, the conjecture asks for a member almost entirely inside X, m(1 - L m^{-1}), which is Conjecture 8.3 = FKNP's Theorem 1.6 up to constants. Conjecture 8.4 interpolates with the exponential rate exp(-s/L) in s = p/delta.
obstruction: The FKNP/ALWZ lemma is stated for hypergraphs (uniform measures on families with multiplicity) and its per-round bound is on the expected size of the leftover, not on the spread of the leftover family conditional on the previous rounds' choices; passing from expectation to the exponential tail in the number of rounds needs the leftover family to remain spread with a parameter that does not degrade with r, which is asserted in the iteration but with a loss of constants that may compound; I did not verify the compounding.
result: Reduction to the FKNP iteration. The proof of FKNP's Theorem 1.6 (after Alweiss-Lovett-Wu-Zhang) is iterative: a random set of density of order 1/kappa = delta 'eats' a constant fraction of a typical member of the spread family, and the family of leftovers, appropriately reweighted, is again spread with a comparable parameter, so that after r rounds (total density r delta) the leftover of some member has size at most m c^r for a constant c < 1; running log m rounds eliminates the member. Stopping after s = p/delta rounds gives a member with at most m c^{s} points outside X, i.e. E_p(B) >= m(1 - c^{s}) = m(1 - exp(-s/L)), which is Conjecture 8.4 provided the per-round loss is a fixed constant factor c independent of the round. In FKNP's Lemma 3.1 the per-round statement is in expectation over the spread family with a small failure probability; whether the failure probabilities accumulate only additively (fine, they are summable geometrically) and whether the constant c is uniform across rounds are the two points to check, and if both hold Conjecture 8.4 is a corollary of the published argument with the same constants.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: (8.1) implies alpha delta <= p/L, so W_alpha(nu) is dominated by mu_p on cylinders with a factor L^{card I} to spare; the k-subset uniform measure passes the test for every L >= 1.
method: Same starting point as for Conjecture 7.9: cylinder domination is automatic and cheap. With nu delta-spread, W_alpha(nu)(H_I) = alpha^{card I} nu(H_I) <= (alpha delta)^{card I}, and (8.1) gives alpha <= 1 - (1-p)^{1/(L delta)} <= p/(L delta) (since 1 - (1-p)^x <= px), so alpha delta <= p/L and the cylinder marginals of the thinned measure are dominated by those of mu_{p/L}, a factor L^{card I} below mu_p. The conjecture upgrades this to all up-classes, uniformly in card S.
obstruction: As for 7.9, there is no tensorisation of domination for non-product nu, and the only route the source offers is the multiplicative strengthening (Conjecture 9.1) whose stability properties (Theorem 9.2) are what make 8.5 believable; a proof would presumably go through 9.1 or through an entirely new coupling construction (Proposition 7.11's push-down coupling).
result: Why the dimension-freeness is plausible: the thinning parameter alpha is allowed to be close to 1 only when delta card S... no: (8.1) is independent of card S, and for nu spread with delta of order 1/M (like the singleton example) alpha may be close to 1 - e^{-pM/L}, essentially 1 when pM is large; then W_alpha(nu) is close to nu itself and the conjecture says a (1/M)-spread measure is nearly dominated by mu_p as soon as pM >> 1, which is the regime where mu_p-random sets have many points and any spread measure 'looks small' against them: for an up-class A, nu(A) is at most the probability that a nu-random set (which has at most... spread implies E card J <= ... no bound on size!)... the singleton example shows the mechanism: nu lives on tiny sets, A = {X != emptyset} has mu_p(A) close to 1, fine. A candidate stress test: nu uniform on the k-subsets, (k/M)-spread, so (8.1) allows alpha up to 1 - (1-p)^{M/(Lk)}; the up-class A = {X : card X >= k}: W_alpha(nu)(A) = alpha^k versus mu_p(A) = P(Bin(M,p) >= k); with alpha^k <= exp(-k (1-p)^{M/(Lk)}) and P(Bin(M,p) >= k) >= 1/2 once pM >= k, the inequality alpha^k <= mu_p(A) holds comfortably when pM >= k, and when pM << k both sides are small and the comparison is between exp(-k e^{-pM/(Lk)}) and a binomial tail exp(-k log(k/(epM)))-ish: the conjecture requires k e^{-pM/(Lk)} >= k log(k/(epM)) - O(1), i.e. e^{-pM/(Lk)} >= log(k/(epM)), which FAILS when pM/k is a large constant times L log log... wait, pM/k large means the first regime; take pM/k = 1/(2L) small: LHS = e^{-1/2}, RHS = log(2L/e) > e^{-1/2} for L >= 2: so for k-subset measures the conjecture predicts alpha^k <= P(Bin(M,p) >= k) with p = k/(2LM), which reads exp(-k(1 - (1-p)^{M/(Lk)})) hmm I conflated; redoing: alpha = 1 - (1-p)^{M/(Lk)} = 1 - exp(-pM/(Lk)(1+o(1))) = 1 - e^{-1/(2L^2)} = 1/(2L^2) + ...; alpha^k = (2L^2)^{-k}; mu_p(A) = P(Bin(M, k/(2LM)) >= k) = exp(-k log(2L e^{-1}... )) = roughly (e/(2L))^k; comparison (2L^2)^{-k} <= (e/(2L))^k holds for L >= 1. Consistent. So the k-subset test passes with the constant L absorbing everything.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: (9.2) for A = complement of H_I forces nu(H_I) <= (p/alpha)^{card I}; the conjecture asserts sufficiency of the alpha p-spread condition.
method: Take (9.2) as the working form: for every down-class A, log mu_p(A) <= sum_X nu({X}) log theta_{X,alpha}(A), i.e. the log-probability of a down-class under mu_p is at most its nu-average log-probability under alpha-thinnings of nu-random sets. Necessity of the spread condition: for A = complement of H_I one gets 1 - p^{card I} <= (1 - alpha^{card I})^{nu(H_I)}, which forces nu(H_I) <= (p/alpha)^{card I} up to constants, so the conjecture says that this necessary condition (with p/alpha replaced by alpha p, a loss of alpha^2) is sufficient.
obstruction: The conjecture's difficulty is in down-classes that are neither small (few configurations) nor 'monotone-simple': the source's Section 10 shows that classes built by iterated block unions/intersections satisfy much more than 9.1 (they lie in C_gamma), and the only classes outside that reach are the symmetric ones (thresholds, Problem 10.9; orbit classes) for which log(1 - zeta_t(A)) has no polynomial majorant known; equally, the only spread measures outside Theorem 9.2's reach are orbit measures like the triangle measure above, where I could only test two down-classes.
result: A test outside the block constructions: nu uniform on the edge sets of triangles of the complete graph K_N (S = edge set, M = binom(N,2)). Spread: nu(H_I) = 0 unless I is contained in a triangle; for one edge nu(H_I) = 3/M, for a triangle 1/binom(N,3), so nu is delta-spread with delta of order 1/N... (delta^3 >= 6/N^3 and delta >= 6/N^2), i.e. the conjecture applies when alpha p >= c/N. Down-class A = {graphs with at most 2 edges}: mu_p(A) = P(Bin(M,p) <= 2), theta_{X,alpha}(A) = 1 - alpha^3 for every triangle X, and (9.2) reads log P(Bin(M,p) <= 2) <= log(1 - alpha^3), which holds since the left side is at most -pM/2 + O(log(pM)) and the right side is -alpha^3 - O(alpha^6): the inequality -pM/2 <= -alpha^3 is pM >= 2 alpha^3, implied by alpha p >= c/N (which gives pM >= c N alpha^{-1}/2 >> alpha^3). Down-class A = {triangle-free graphs}: log mu_p(A) is of order -p^3 N^3 (Janson) and log theta = log(1 - alpha^3) = -alpha^3 - ...; (9.2) needs p^3 N^3 >= c alpha^3, i.e. pN >= c alpha, implied by alpha p >= c'/N. Both tests pass with room, for the same reason: the spread condition alpha p >= c/N forces pN large, and then any down-class that a thinned triangle is likely to satisfy is unlikely for G(N,p) at the exponential scale.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: P(t) = sum_i t_i always satisfies (10.1); the content of C_gamma is the tightness condition (10.2) at gamma q.
method: Understand C_gamma as a two-sided polynomial approximation problem for the function F_A(t) = -log(1 - zeta_t(A)) = -log P(zeta_t-random set is not in A): F_A is nondecreasing in each t_i, F_A(0) = 0, and by inclusion-exclusion 1 - zeta_t(A) = sum_{X not in A} prod_{i in X}(1 - e^{-t_i}) prod_{i not in X} e^{-t_i}; the majorant P must be a positive polynomial with no constant term dominating F_A everywhere while touching it at the point gamma q up to the factor gamma.
obstruction: The definition is quantified over all q, and the required polynomial changes with q; there is no candidate construction of P from the structure of A beyond the block recursion (Proposition 10.5), and for symmetric classes the natural symmetric polynomials of bounded degree seem insufficient when k is large (the survival probability of a threshold class is a binomial tail whose log has the entropy shape, not a polynomial shape), which is why the source separates Problem 10.9.
result: Three observations. (a) The class C_gamma is nonempty and closed under the block operations, so all read-once formulas built from AND ({S}) and OR ({X != emptyset}) gates are in C_gamma: this includes every 'tribes'-type class. (b) For the threshold classes A_k = {card X >= k} (Problem 10.9) the function is F(t) = -log P(Poisson-binomial(1 - e^{-t_i}) < k), and for k = 1 it is sum t_i (Proposition 10.4); for k = 2 and card S = 2 the class is {S} (Theorem 10.6); the first new case is k = 2, card S = 3 (majority of three), where F(t) = sum_i t_i - log(1 + sum_i (e^{t_i} - 1)) and one can test the definition numerically: with q = (q,q,q) symmetric, the natural candidate P is symmetric of degree at most 3 in the elementary symmetric functions, and (10.1)-(10.2) become a finite semi-algebraic feasibility problem in the three coefficients for each q; I did not run it, but it is a computation that would give the best gamma for majority-of-three and would show whether gamma must degrade with k, which is the content of Problem 10.9. (c) A negative answer to 10.2 would need an up-class with F_A having a 'non-polynomial' shape, e.g. a class whose survival probability decays like exp(-t^{1/2}) in a direction, but F_A is a finite sum of exponentials in the t_i and is always bounded by the linear function sum_i t_i... no: F_A <= -log(1 - zeta_t(S-complement...)) hmm, F_A(t) <= F_{{X != emptyset}}(t) = sum_i t_i when A is contained in {X != emptyset}, always true for A != everything; so P(t) = sum t_i satisfies (10.1) for every up-class, and the whole content of Problem 10.2 is (10.2): the linear majorant must be replaced by one that is tight at gamma q within the factor gamma, i.e. the question is whether F_A(gamma q)... whether some positive polynomial squeezed between F_A and its value at gamma q exists; for the class {S}, F_{{S}}(q) = -log prod(1 - e^{-q_i}) is of order sum e^{-q_i} for large q while the linear majorant is sum q_i, far too big, which is why Theorem 10.6 needs the cross terms t_i t_j.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: F_{A_k}(t, ..., t) ~ (Nt)^k/k! for small t and ~ (N-k+1) t for large t, so the majorant must interpolate degree k and degree 1 while being tight at gamma q.
method: Reduce to the symmetric case and to a one-parameter family. For A_k = {card X >= k}, F(t) = -log P(sum_i B_i < k) with B_i independent Bernoulli(1 - e^{-t_i}). By symmetry one expects the optimal polynomial for a symmetric q = (q, ..., q) to be symmetric, P(t) = sum_{j} beta_j e_j(t) with e_j the elementary symmetric polynomials, and (10.1) then has to hold for all t, not only symmetric ones, which is the real constraint (Theorem 10.7 for k = 2 = card S is exactly the two-variable version).
obstruction: Deciding the question requires either a uniform construction of P for all k (the block recursion does not produce threshold classes) or a lower bound argument showing the best gamma_k tends to 0; the latter would need a dual certificate (a measure on t's against which no positive polynomial can be tight at gamma q), and neither is available; a numerical experiment for k = 2, N = 3 and k = 3, N = 5 would show the trend and is the natural next step.
result: For k = 1 the answer is gamma = 1 with P = e_1. For k = card S = N (the class {S}) the source proves some gamma > 0 with P a combination of e_1 and e_2-type cross terms, and leaves gamma = 1 open. Interpolating: for general k the survival function at symmetric t = (t, ..., t) is P(Bin(N, 1 - e^{-t}) < k), whose negative log grows like N t for t small (below the threshold t ~ k/N) and like k log(N t/k)-type... no: for large t, P(Bin < k) ~ binom(N, k-1) e^{-t(N-k+1)}, so F ~ (N - k + 1) t - log binom(N,k-1): linear growth with slope N - k + 1 at large t and slope N at small t (F ~ N t for t << k/N... check: P(Bin(N,1-e^{-t}) < k) for tiny t is 1 - P(Bin >= k) ~ 1 - (Nt)^k/k!, so F ~ (Nt)^k/k!, degree k in t). So the polynomial majorant must be of degree at least k near the origin (to match (Nt)^k/k!) and must be dominated by a linear function at infinity, which a positive polynomial of degree k cannot be unless its degree-k coefficient is tiny: (10.1) forces beta_{e_k} <= 1/k!-ish while (10.2) at gamma q with q small forces P(gamma q) <= -gamma log(1 - zeta_q(A)) ~ gamma (Nq)^k/k!, so beta_{e_k} (gamma N q)^k/... = beta_{e_k} binom(N,k) (gamma q)^k <= gamma (Nq)^k/k!, i.e. gamma^{k-1} beta_{e_k} binom(N,k) <= N^k/k!, fine for beta_{e_k} = 1/k! up to constants: gamma^{k-1} <= 1 + o(1): no obstruction at small q. The tension is at intermediate q (q of order k/N, the threshold of the class) where F crosses from degree-k to linear behaviour, and the polynomial P must track F within the factor gamma at the single point gamma q while staying above F everywhere; for k = 2 Theorem 10.7 does it by hand with a case analysis, and the general k requires a positivity certificate for F(t) <= P(t) that seems to need degree growing with k, so gamma may have to shrink with k, which would answer Problem 10.9 negatively as stated (uniform gamma).

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: At b lambda_2^2 = 1 the root signal in the census is b^{n/2} while the census fluctuation is sqrt(n) b^{n/2}: signal/noise = n^{-1/2}.
method: Reduce the conjecture to a local limit theorem for the critical multitype Galton-Watson census. Write the census c_n as a vector in R^q and project it on a left eigenvector v of M for lambda_2 (assume first lambda_2 real, simple). Given the root state i, E[<v, c_n>] = b^n lambda_2^n v_i, while the variance of <v, c_n> is of order n b^n at the critical point b lambda_2^2 = 1 (the innovations of the b^k vertices of generation k propagate to level n with factor b^{n-k} lambda_2^{n-k} in the projection, so they contribute variance b^k (b^{n-k} lambda_2^{n-k})^2 = b^n (b lambda_2^2)^{n-k} = b^n each at criticality; summing over k gives n b^n). So the mean separation between roots i and j is b^{n/2}|v_i - v_j| against a standard deviation of order sqrt(n) b^{n/2}: the signal-to-noise ratio of the LINEAR census statistic is of order n^{-1/2} and tends to 0.
obstruction: Three things are missing. (1) A local CLT in total variation for a critical multitype branching process (the Kesten-Stigum critical CLT [23] is a convergence in distribution, and the lattice/aperiodicity conditions on the census need the local-limit version); (2) the case of a complex or non-simple lambda_2 (Jordan blocks change the variance growth from n b^n to n^{2r-1} b^n for a block of size r, and a complex pair makes the projection two-dimensional and rotating); (3) the coupling step of [30] uses b lambda_2^2 < 1 to make the root-dependent shift o(b^{n/2}), and at criticality the shift is exactly of order b^{n/2}, so the argument must be run at the scale sqrt(n) b^{n/2} instead, which is where the local CLT has to be uniform.
result: The linear statistic fails at criticality, and the total variation distance between the two Gaussian limits (same covariance, means differing by b^{n/2} in a direction of standard deviation sqrt(n) b^{n/2}) is of order n^{-1/2} -> 0. Hence the conjecture follows from a LOCAL limit theorem in total variation for the critical census: d_TV(law(c_n | root i), law(c_n | root j)) -> 0 would follow if the lattice-valued vector c_n, centred and scaled, converged to its Gaussian limit in total variation with the root-dependent shift being o(1) on the scale of the fluctuations. This is exactly the structure of the proof in [30] for the non-critical case b lambda_2^2 < 1 as the source describes it (coupling of c_n^i and c_n^j to within o(b^{n/2}) plus a local CLT), with the extra input at criticality being the n b^n variance growth.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: For q = 3: non-reconstruction for lambda <= (1 + sqrt(1 + 24 b))/(6 b), census reconstruction for lambda > b^{-1/2}; the ratio of the two endpoints tends to sqrt(2/3).
method: Locate the window in which the residual case q = 3 lives, for each b, from the two bounds the source itself states. Non-reconstruction (PDF p. 9, from [30]): b (1 - q epsilon)^2 / (1 - (q-2) epsilon) <= 1. With lambda = lambda_2 = 1 - q epsilon and q = 3 this reads b lambda^2 <= (2 + lambda)/3, i.e. 3 b lambda^2 - lambda - 2 <= 0, i.e. lambda <= lambda_nr(b) := (1 + sqrt(1 + 24 b)) / (6 b). Reconstruction (census, Theorem 4.1): lambda > b^{-1/2}.
obstruction: Deciding the b = 2, q = 3 window needs the exact reconstruction threshold on the binary tree, which the recursion methods of the source (Section 6.2) only handle for the binary symmetric channel; Sly's argument is a large-degree expansion (Gaussian approximation of the recursion) and does not reach b = 2. Numerically one could iterate the belief-propagation distributional recursion on the binary tree at epsilon = 0.10 and 0.11 to see whether the root posterior degenerates; that is the concrete next step, not done here.
result: For q = 3 the conjecture can only hold at a pair (b, lambda) with lambda in the window (lambda_nr(b), b^{-1/2}]. Numerically: b = 2: (2/3, 0.7071]; b = 3: (0.5302, 0.5774]; b = 4: (0.4520, 0.5000]; b = 10: (0.2754, 0.3162]. As b -> infinity, lambda_nr(b) ~ sqrt(24 b)/(6 b) = (sqrt(2/3)) b^{-1/2} = 0.8165 b^{-1/2}, so the window (0.8165 b^{-1/2}, b^{-1/2}] does not close in relative terms; Sly's theorem (the bound is tight for large b) therefore cannot come from the coupling bound and is genuinely stronger. For the residual open case the conjecture asks whether some small b has a solvable point inside this window; for b = 2 the window is lambda in (0.6667, 0.7071], i.e. epsilon in [0.0976, 0.1111).

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: M_2 K = K M_1 iff the average row of K is uniform on q_1; the per-edge Markov property additionally forces K deterministic, hence q_1 | q_2.
method: Ask whether the 'obvious' case (q_1 divides q_2, lumping the q_2 symbols into q_1 classes of equal size) is the only way to realise the q_1-process as a vertex-wise function of the q_2-process, i.e. whether a proof by degradation can exist. Write M_q = lambda I + (1 - lambda) U_q with U_q the matrix with all entries 1/q. Suppose K is a q_2 x q_1 stochastic kernel applied independently at every vertex, sigma_1(v) = K(sigma_2(v)). For sigma_1 to be the M_1-broadcast one needs, for a child w of v, that the law of sigma_1(w) given sigma_2(v) = c equals M_1(a', .) for every a' with K(c, a') > 0 (the noise at w is independent of the noise at v).
obstruction: A proof must compare the two tree measures globally (e.g. through the distributional belief-propagation recursions: the q-state recursion at fixed lambda has a fixed point structure whose non-trivial fixed point should move monotonically with q), or through a coupling that uses several levels at once. The census component is identical for M_1 and M_2 (same lambda, Theorem 4.1), so the conjecture is only about the regime b lambda^2 < 1, where the recursion is non-linear and no monotonicity in q is known.
result: Compute (M_2 K)(c, .) = lambda K(c, .) + (1 - lambda) pi, where pi is the average row of K (since U_{q_2} K has all rows equal to pi). The required identity is lambda K(c, .) + (1 - lambda) pi = lambda delta_{a'} + (1 - lambda) u_{q_1} for every a' in the support of K(c, .), which forces K(c, .) = delta_{a'} (K deterministic) and pi = u_{q_1} (uniform average row). A deterministic K with uniform average row is a partition of q_2 symbols into q_1 classes of equal size, so q_1 | q_2. So: the only vertex-wise independent degradation of the q_2-broadcast onto the q_1-broadcast at equal lambda is the lumping, and Conjecture 4 for q_1 not dividing q_2 cannot be proved by a per-vertex channel comparison. Intertwining alone (M_2 K = K M_1, which holds iff the average row of K is uniform, with no divisibility needed) is not enough because the induced process is not Markov along edges.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Window for the 3-state model on T_b: (1 + sqrt(1 + 24 b))/(6 b) < lambda <= b^{-1/2} (ferro) and -b^{-1/2} <= lambda < -(sqrt(1 + 24 b) - 1)/(6 b) (antiferro).
method: Tabulate the open window for each b from the source's own bounds (the same algebra as in F0117 for the ferromagnetic side, lambda > 0): non-reconstruction for lambda <= lambda_nr(b) = (1 + sqrt(1 + 24 b))/(6 b), reconstruction for lambda > b^{-1/2}. On the antiferromagnetic side lambda < 0 the coupling bound of the source becomes b lambda^2 <= 1 - (q - 2) epsilon with epsilon = (1 - lambda)/3 > 1/3, i.e. b lambda^2 <= (2 + lambda)/3 again, so for lambda < 0: 3 b lambda^2 - lambda - 2 <= 0, lambda >= -( -1 + sqrt(1 + 24 b))/(6 b) = -(sqrt(1 + 24b) - 1)/(6 b).
obstruction: The exact threshold inside the window requires analysing the belief-propagation distributional recursion for the 3-state channel on a small-degree tree, for which no closed criterion exists (the source: 'The only case in which this iteration was analyzed is the symmetric binary channel'). A numerical population-dynamics iteration at b = 2, 3 would give a conjectural threshold; a proof would need a contraction argument tailored to q = 3 at small b, which is what Sly's large-degree Gaussian approximation replaces.
result: Open windows (ferromagnetic): b = 2: lambda in (0.6667, 0.7071]; b = 3: (0.5302, 0.5774]; b = 4: (0.4520, 0.5000]. Antiferromagnetic: b = 2: lambda in [-0.7071, -0.5000); b = 3: [-0.5774, -0.4191); b = 4: [-0.5000, -0.3687) (note the antiferromagnetic window is wider: the coupling bound is weaker there, and Mossel-Sly-Sohn's abstract says the q = 4 antiferromagnetic tightness depends on the degree, so the antiferromagnetic side is the more likely place for a non-Kesten-Stigum threshold at small b). Everything outside these windows is settled by the two bounds; inside them the answer for small b is open, and Sly's theorem says the ferromagnetic window collapses to its right endpoint for large b.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Frozen recursion p -> sum_k (-1)^k C(q-1,k)(1 - kp/(q-1))^b ~ (1 - e^{-bp/(q-1)})^{q-1}; positive fixed point iff roughly b > (q-1) log(q-1).
method: Derive the q log q scale from the 'frozen' recursion, which is the coupon-collector argument the source alludes to made quantitative. Say a vertex is determined if its colour is forced by the (determined) colours of its children: this happens when the children exhibit all q - 1 other colours. If each child is determined independently with probability p and a determined child's colour is uniform on the q - 1 colours other than the parent's, then the parent is determined with probability P(all q - 1 colours appear among Bin(b, p) children) = sum_{k=0}^{q-1} (-1)^k C(q-1, k) (1 - k p/(q-1))^b.
obstruction: For fixed small q (say q = 3, 4, 5) the frozen recursion is not sharp and the true threshold sits between q - 1 and the frozen-recursion value; determining it exactly needs the full BP recursion on the (q - 1)-simplex, for which no exact solution is known. The natural test case is q = 3: is 3-colouring reconstruction solvable on the binary tree (b = 2)? The coupling bound gives non-reconstruction for b <= 2 = q - 1, so b = 2 is NOT solvable; b = 3 is the first open value for q = 3 (frozen recursion needs b > 2 log 2 + ... ~ 3.4, inconclusive).
result: For large b and q with b p/(q - 1) = s fixed the right-hand side is (1 - e^{-s})^{q-1} + o(1), so the frozen recursion has a fixed point p* > 0 iff the map p -> (1 - e^{-b p/(q-1)})^{q-1} has a fixed point away from 0. Near p = 1 the condition is (q - 1) e^{-b/(q-1)} < 1 - o(1), i.e. b > (q - 1) log(q - 1) + O(q): this reproduces the q log q reconstruction threshold of the coupon-collector argument, one step below Sly's q(log q + log log q + 1) (the log log q term comes from the fact that the parent's colour need not be fully determined, only biased). On the non-reconstruction side the source's coupling bound b|lambda_2| <= 1 gives only b <= q - 1, and the census bound b lambda_2^2 > 1 gives reconstruction only for b > (q - 1)^2, both far from the truth: colourings are the extreme example of the census being useless.

author: claude-prob1000-F-0908
key_identity: Single-step odds (1 - p)/p equal the two-colour matching probability 2^{-2} exactly at p = 4/5; for k-step excursions the C(2k,k) ~ 4^k entropy of shapes cancels the 2^{-2k} matching cost, so the threshold is a critical balance.
method: Isolate what is open and what mechanism sets 4/5. For p > 1/2 the walk is transient to the right; the number of returns to 0 is geometric with success probability 1 - 2(1 - p) = 2p - 1, and Y_0 = C_0 is re-observed at each return.
